name: relaybell
author: relaybell

sections.description:
relaybell turns visitors into subscribers you can bring back with one click — no
app, and no email address needed. A notification reaches them even when your site
isn’t open, and each one can carry the product or post that this subscriber is
likely to want, picked from what they viewed, read and bought on your site.

Connect in about a minute. Then new posts go out as a push when you publish,
abandoned carts get a reminder, sold-out products tell their waitlist when they’re
back, and you see which notifications brought visitors and sales back.

relaybell is free with every feature for up to 500 subscribers; bigger lists have
monthly plans (see https://relaybell.com/pricing).

What you get

  • More returning visitors, without paying for every click.
  • Sales you’d otherwise lose: cart reminders showing the shopper’s own items,
    back-in-stock, price-drop, low-stock and launch alerts go out on their own.
  • Order updates by notification: buyers opt in on the thank-you page and hear
    when their order is confirmed, shipped and delivered; cash-on-delivery orders
    can be confirmed with one tap.
  • Notifications people open: recommendations matched to each subscriber,
    delivered at the hour they usually read.
  • Written and timed by AI: ready-made automations write each message and send
    it when that shopper usually looks.
  • Clear numbers: delivered, clicked and revenue for every notification.
  • Honest numbers: switch on a comparison group to see the sales relaybell
    really added.

Features

Grow subscribers

  • One-click Connect to relaybell — sign in or create a free account, approve
    your site, done. Nothing to copy or paste.
  • Opt-in prompt as a slide-in, bar, modal or the browser’s own prompt; shown after
    a delay, on scroll, on exit intent or on a click; A/B-test its wording.
  • Topics subscribers choose, and an “Alert me when it’s back” button (it reads
    “Alert me when it launches” on products marked Coming soon (relaybell)).
  • Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Samsung Internet and Brave on desktop and Android;
    Safari on macOS 13+ and on iPhone/iPad (iOS 16.4+, from the Home Screen).

Personalized notifications

  • Catalog sync: published WooCommerce products and blog posts are sent to
    relaybell in the background and updated within about a minute of each change.
  • Per-subscriber interests, learned from what each subscriber views, reads,
    adds to the cart and buys on your site — your own first-party data only.
  • Product and article recommendations: put {rec.title}, {rec.price} or
    {rec.summary} in a notification and each subscriber gets their own pick.
    Out-of-stock products are skipped at send time.
  • GA4 events with no code: relaybell can use the Google Analytics 4
    e-commerce events your site already sends through Google Tag Manager or gtag.js.
  • Smart timing: delivery at each subscriber’s usual hour, in their time zone,
    within your quiet hours and frequency cap.
  • Past orders (optional): import 90 days of orders for a head start.

Automations & journeys

  • Push new posts on publish, with the featured image, for the post types you pick.
  • Welcome series and custom journeys with delays and branches; subscribers leave
    when they buy.
  • Automations triggered by anything a subscriber does on your site.
  • Recurring campaigns, RSS-to-push, scheduling and A/B-tested notifications.

WooCommerce

  • Cart reminders for shoppers who added to cart or started checkout.
  • Back in stock alerts to the product’s waitlist.
  • Price drop alerts to shoppers who viewed, carted or wait-listed it.
  • Order updates: thank-you and follow-up messages after purchases and refunds.
  • Revenue attribution, with each order counted once.
  • Classic checkout, the Checkout block and HPOS.

Analytics & delivery health

  • Delivered, clicks, conversions and revenue per notification; CSV export.
  • Delivery health: why a notification didn’t arrive, in plain words.
  • Conversion goals with a funnel.

Privacy & control

  • Consent: Google Consent Mode, or wait for your cookie banner’s consent.
  • GDPR: export or erase everything held about a subscriber.
  • Identity verification: logged-in visitors’ IDs are signed by your server, so
    nobody can pose as a customer to get their notifications. On from the start.
  • A switch for each WooCommerce event and for catalog sync.
  • Suggested privacy policy text for your site, under Settings → Privacy.

Works with

WooCommerce, Google Tag Manager and GA4, Zapier, the relaybell REST API and
webhooks, server SDKs for Node.js and PHP, and common page-cache plugins.

Why relaybell

  • Set up in about a minute: one click, no keys, no code, no theme changes.
  • It checks itself: the status panel tests eight things — connection, HTTPS,
    the script, the service worker, your browser, your public pages, page caches
    and sign-in IDs — and says how to fix anything that isn’t right.
  • Never slows your site: events are sent after the page is built; the catalog
    and past orders go out in small background batches; saving a post never waits
    for relaybell.
  • Built for real hosting: the service worker is a static file in the plugin
    folder (no clash with PWA plugins, any permalink setting), its address avoids
    patterns hosting firewalls block, and 13 common page caches are cleared when
    your set-up changes.
  • Secure by default: signed visitor IDs, HTTPS-only connection settings, and
    the API key is cancelled when you disconnect.
  • Open: GPL plugin, documented REST API and webhooks, CSV export.

Your data

Nothing is sent until you connect. The catalog holds only what is public on your
site — never password-protected, private or hidden items, and no customer data.
Activity is recorded only for visitors who subscribed. Order events carry the
customer’s email (or your hashed ID) only to find their subscription — no names,
addresses or phone numbers. Past orders are sent only when you ask. Every request
is listed under “External services”.

External services

This plugin connects to relaybell (https://relaybell.com), a web push
notification service operated by Nexistech. relaybell is required: browser push
notifications can’t be stored or delivered without a push service, and this
plugin is the WordPress client for it. You need a relaybell account and API key.

1. Browser SDK (https://relaybell.com/relaybell-sdk.js)

Loaded on every front-end page once a Project ID is saved, so visitors can opt in.
On each page view it also fetches your project’s public settings (GET
https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/config: push key, prompt and
on-site message settings). Browsers send their normal request data (IP address,
user agent, your site’s address). If you use them, it also reports, without
personal data, which A/B prompt version was shown (POST …/prompt-event) and
on-site message views and clicks (POST …/onsite-event).

2. Subscribing (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/subscriptions)

When a visitor accepts the notification prompt: the browser’s push endpoint URL
and encryption keys, the page URL, language, time zone, prompt version, and your
topics or tags (for logged-in users, their WordPress role). The service worker
re-sends a subscription the browser replaced. Topic choices made in the box
opened by RelayBell.showPreferences() are saved (GET/POST …/preferences).
For a logged-in visitor (never an administrator) who opted in, their account email
is sent as externalId, with a userHash signature (see 9). Hash it with the
relaybell_external_id filter, or turn off “Link subscribers to their account
email”.

3. Publish pushes (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications)

With “Send on publish” on: the post’s title, first 20 words, permalink, featured
image URL and (with “Category → topic”) topic. Never for password-protected posts.

4. WooCommerce events from your server (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/events)

With your API key, at the end of the request that caused them: purchase and
checkout.started (order id and number, total, currency, the payment method’s id
such as “cod”, and up to 50 products: id, name, category, unit price, quantity); order.refunded (order id and number,
amount, currency); order.status_changed (order id and number, the new and old
status, your shop’s address, and for a registered customer the “view order” page
address); cart.updated (the added product’s name, id and URL, cart value and
currency, and up to 10 cart products: id, name, image URL, page URL, price,
quantity); signup (user id); back_in_stock (product name, id, URL, and whether
it was marked Coming soon), price_drop (product name, id, URL, and old and new
price) and low_stock (product name, id, URL and stock count, when a managed
stock count falls to 50 or fewer). All on by default; each can be turned off
under Settings → relaybell. While “Link subscribers to their account email”
is on, the customer’s email (account email, else the billing email, or your
relaybell_external_id value) is sent with purchase, checkout.started,
order.status_changed, cart.updated, signup and order.refunded; with it
off, they’re sent without it and cart.updated not at all. cart.updated is only
sent for logged-in shoppers. back_in_stock, price_drop and low_stock never
include customer data.

5. Visitor activity (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/events)

From the browser, only for visitors subscribed to your notifications:
waitlist.join (the “Notify me” button), product.viewed (a product page, while
Price drop or “Send my products” is on: product id, category, price, currency,
brand, page URL, image) and content.viewed (a post, while “Send my posts” is
on: post id, title, type, category, up to 10 tags, permalink), followed once by
content.read when they scrolled 75% of the page or stayed 30 seconds, and
search_submitted (on a search results page, while the “Still looking for…?”
automation is on in relaybell, for visitors subscribed to your notifications or
signed in: the words searched and the results page address with only its search
parameters; words that look like an email address, a phone number or a link are not
kept). Each
carries your project id, the push endpoint URL and, for a logged-in visitor with
“Link subscribers…” on, their externalId and userHash.

On the order-received (thank-you) page, while order updates are on in your
relaybell dashboard, the buyer can choose “Yes, notify me”: their browser sends
(POST …/projects/{project id}/order-link) the push endpoint URL and the order’s
id and number, payment method, total, currency, status, your shop’s address and
time, signed on your server with your identity secret (see 9). The signed order is
printed in that page only with the order’s own key in the address, and never for
failed, cancelled or refunded orders. No name, email or address is included.

6. Delivery and click reports (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications/{id}/receipt and /click)

From the service worker: the notification id, a signed token and the
subscription’s id — no page content or personal data.

7. Connecting (https://relaybell.com/connect/wordpress, POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/connect/exchange)

Connect to relaybell sends the administrator’s browser to relaybell with your
site’s address and name, the wp-admin return address and a one-time security
value. Your server then trades the one-time code (with your site address) for
your Project ID and an API key, saved in your database.

8. Admin status and test push (https://relaybell.com/api/v1/…)

From your server, with your API key: subscriber count (GET /stats), that the
Project ID matches the key (GET /me), and when relaybell last ran on your pages
(GET /setup-status); the Plugins screen re-checks an unverified account at most
hourly. The administrator’s browser fetches the script and public settings to
check they aren’t blocked, and your server occasionally fetches your own home page
to detect a stale page cache (that request stays on your site). Subscribe this
browser subscribes the admin’s browser (see 2) and marks it as a test device
(POST /test-devices: its endpoint URL); Send test push sends a test to test
devices only (POST /test-devices/send: test title, text, home page address); a
“send test to my device” link registers that browser (POST /test-devices/claim:
the code and endpoint URL). Advanced → relaybell host changes where these
requests go (https only).

9. Identity verification (GET and PUT https://relaybell.com/api/v1/identity)

Your server fetches your project’s identity secret — when you connect, when you
open Settings → relaybell, and daily — and the first time asks relaybell to
accept only verified sign-in IDs (changeable in your relaybell dashboard). The
secret signs logged-in visitors’ IDs on your server and never appears in your
pages. No visitor data is sent.

10. Disconnecting (DELETE https://relaybell.com/api/v1/keys/current)

Disconnect cancels the API key one-click Connect created (only the key is
sent). A key entered by hand is left alone.

11. Catalog (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/catalog/items and /catalog/items/delete)

So notifications can recommend them, your server sends the public details of
published WooCommerce products (“Send my products”) and posts (“Send my posts”),
both on by default: id, title, permalink, image URL, price and sale price with
the currency, category path, brand, tags, a short plain-text summary, stock
status and publication date. Never password-protected, private, draft or hidden
items, and no customer data. WP-Cron sends them in the background, 100 per run:
everything when you connect, update the plugin, change these settings or click
Sync now, and weekly; and each product or post you publish, edit,
unpublish, trash or delete within about a minute (for the last three, only its
id). Turning a switch off removes those items from relaybell.

12. Past orders (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/events/import)

Only after an administrator clicks Import the last 90 days of orders: that
period’s paid orders as purchase events, 50 per background run — the details of
a live purchase (see 4), the payment date, and the customer’s email (or your
relaybell_external_id value) to find their subscription. relaybell keeps only
orders of customers who already get your notifications, never counts an order
twice, and gets no names, addresses or phone numbers.

Nothing is sent until you connect (or save a Project ID and API key manually).

Service provider: Nexistech (https://nexistech.in)
Terms of service: https://relaybell.com/terms
Privacy policy: https://relaybell.com/privacy
Data processing agreement: https://relaybell.com/dpa
sections.installation:
1. In your WordPress admin go to Plugins → Add New, search for relaybell,
    then click Install Now and Activate. (Or upload the ZIP from
    Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin.)
  2. Go to Settings → relaybell and click Connect to relaybell. Sign in (or
    create a free account), approve your site, and you’ll land back in WordPress
    connected.
  3. Optionally turn on Send on publish and pick which post types push.
  4. Your products and posts start syncing to relaybell in the background. With
    WooCommerce, you can also click Import the last 90 days of orders.

Your site must use HTTPS — browsers only allow push notifications on secure
sites (and on localhost for testing). The status panel tells you if anything
needs attention.

The WooCommerce integration loads by itself when WooCommerce is active — there is
nothing extra to set up.
sections.faq:
Do I need WooCommerce?

No. Without WooCommerce you get the opt-in prompt, publish-time pushes and post
recommendations. The commerce features switch on by themselves when WooCommerce
is active.

Do subscribers need to give an email address?

No. Web push works from the browser subscription alone. If a user is logged in,
relaybell also binds their account email as an externalId for richer targeting;
you can substitute a hashed value with the relaybell_external_id filter.

How do recommendations work?

The plugin keeps relaybell’s copy of your catalog up to date (products and posts),
and records what each subscribed visitor opens. relaybell turns that, plus their
cart adds, purchases and notification clicks, into an interest profile per
subscriber. Put {rec.title}, {rec.url}, {rec.price} or {rec.summary} in a
notification — or choose “Recommend a product” in the relaybell composer — and
each subscriber gets their own pick. Someone relaybell doesn’t know yet gets your
popular items.

What exactly is sent for the catalog? Can I leave something out?

The public details of published products and posts: title, link, image, price,
category, brand, tags, a short summary and stock status — see “External
services” (11). Untick Send my products or Send my posts under
Settings → relaybell → Personalization to stop sending them (they are then
removed from relaybell). Developers can leave out single items or change what is
sent with the relaybell_catalog_item filter.

Will syncing slow down my site or my edits?

No. Saving a post or a product only notes its id; WP-Cron sends the changes in
the background within about a minute, and the full catalog goes out 100 items per
run, picking up where it stopped if a run is interrupted. On a site with little
traffic, WP-Cron runs less often, so a large first sync can take a while — the
status on Settings → relaybell shows how far it got.

Can I recommend courses, listings or other custom post types?

Yes. Add your post type with the relaybell_catalog_post_types filter, and use
relaybell_catalog_item_type to send it as a course or listing (it is an
article otherwise).

What does “Import the last 90 days of orders” send? Is it safe to run twice?

The paid orders of the last 90 days, with the same details as a new order’s
purchase event. relaybell keeps only orders from customers who already get your
notifications, and never counts an order twice — not even one it already got
when it was placed — so you can run it again at any time.

How do I send a test notification?

On Settings → relaybell, click Subscribe this browser (allow notifications
when your browser asks), then Send test push. The test goes only to your own
browser — never to your subscribers — and appears within a few seconds. The
settings page then tells you whether it reached this browser, and what to check
if you don’t see it.

If no permission pop-up appears, look for a bell icon in the address bar and
choose Allow. If notifications are blocked, the status panel explains how to
unblock them.

The test push works, but my visitors never get my posts

Most often your relaybell account email isn’t verified yet. Until it is,
relaybell doesn’t send anything to your visitors — new-post pushes, campaigns
and automations are all held back — while test pushes to your own browser still
work. Click the link in the email relaybell sent when you signed up (check your
spam folder), or send it again from your relaybell dashboard. The status panel
and the Plugins screen show a red warning while this is the case.

Also check that Send on publish is turned on (it is off by default) and,
if you use Category → topic, that relaybell has a topic for the post’s
category. Password-protected posts are never pushed.

I use a page cache or a CDN — do I need to do anything?

relaybell’s set-up is part of every page, so a cached page keeps the set-up it
was saved with. When you connect, disconnect, change the connection or update
the plugin, relaybell clears the cache of WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache, W3 Total
Cache, WP Super Cache, SiteGround Speed Optimizer, Breeze, Nginx Helper, Cache
Enabler, WP Fastest Cache, WP-Optimize, Hummingbird, WP Engine and Kinsta. If
your host or a CDN such as Cloudflare caches your pages too, clear that cache
yourself. The status panel warns when visitors still get an older copy, and
shows when relaybell last ran on your public pages. (Developers: other caches
can hook into relaybell_purge_page_caches.)

How does “Category → topic” work?

With it on, each new post is sent only to subscribers who follow the relaybell
topic named like the post’s primary category — for example a topic “Tech News”
for the category tech-news. Create those topics in your relaybell dashboard
(Audience → Topics) first: a post whose category has no matching topic isn’t
pushed. Visitors choose their topics in the box your site opens with
RelayBell.showPreferences() (for example from a “Notification settings” link).

The status panel says my site isn’t on HTTPS

Browsers only allow push notifications on HTTPS sites, plus localhost for
development. Enable HTTPS (most hosts offer a free certificate), and make sure
both addresses under Settings → General start with https://.

Connect doesn’t work on my server

Your server must be able to make outgoing HTTPS requests to relaybell.com. If
your host blocks that, open Advanced on the settings page and enter your
Project ID and an API key from the relaybell dashboard manually.

Does it support HPOS (custom order tables)?

Yes. The plugin declares custom_order_tables compatibility and uses the
WooCommerce CRUD APIs throughout.

Which hooks/filters can I use?

  • relaybell_external_id — swap the account email for a hashed id. Also applied
    to the customer email sent with WooCommerce events and the past-orders import
    ($user is null for a guest order).
  • relaybell_sdk_init — modify the full SDK init options. For a logged-in
    visitor the plugin identified, the userHash for the externalId you return is
    added afterwards.
  • relaybell_user_hash( $external_id ) (function) — the userHash for an id your
    own code passes to relaybell (e.g. to RelayBell.identify( id, hash )), so
    relaybell accepts it while User ID verification is on.
  • relaybell_publish_payload — modify the publish push body.
  • relaybell_category_topic — map a post’s primary category to a relaybell
    topic (its slug, or its id).
  • relaybell_woo_event_payload — modify any commerce event body before sending.
  • relaybell_catalog_post_types — the post types sent to the catalog as content
    (default: post).
  • relaybell_catalog_item_type — a post’s catalog type: article (default),
    course, listing, product or other.
  • relaybell_catalog_item — change a catalog item before it is sent, or return
    null to leave it out.
  • relaybell_catalog_brand_taxonomies — where a product’s brand is read from.
  • relaybell_purge_page_caches (action) — clear a page cache or CDN relaybell
    doesn’t know, whenever relaybell clears page caches.
sections.changelog:
1.10.0

  • When a WooCommerce payment fails, the plugin now tells relaybell, with the order’s
    pay-again link. relaybell uses it for the optional “Payment didn’t go through”
    reminder, which sends the shopper one push to finish their order. It goes with the
    “Checkout started” setting; no payment or card details are sent.

1.9.0

  • Orders now tell relaybell how they were paid: the payment method’s id, such as
    “cod” for cash on delivery (no payment or customer details). relaybell uses it for
    the optional “Ask cash-on-delivery buyers to pay online” automation, which stays off
    until you turn it on.

1.8.0

  • Products whose stock WooCommerce tracks now send their stock count with the
    product (no customer data). relaybell uses it for the optional “Only 3 left”
    note on product pages and for low-stock alerts, and only shows real numbers.

1.7.0

  • Offers in automations (WooCommerce): when you turn on discounts in relaybell
    (Automations → Offers, off by default), the plugin creates a one-time coupon for
    each shopper relaybell sends an offer to: percent off, one use, an expiry date,
    not combinable with other coupons. Requests are signed by relaybell with your
    site’s secret and each one is accepted once. Expired, unused codes are removed
    daily.
  • Purchases now tell relaybell which coupon codes were used, so it can show how
    many orders used an offer.
  • Clearer wording: “Send test notification”, “Alert me” on every back-in-stock
    button, and links that point to the current places in the relaybell dashboard.

1.6.0

  • Simpler settings page. Settings are grouped into New posts, Your store and
    Recommendations; rarely changed options are under “More options”. The store
    section shows only when WooCommerce is active.
  • The status panel’s technical checks are folded into one “Site checks” line
    that says “all good” or how many need attention, and opens by itself when one
    fails.
  • No setting changes: everything you set before stays as it was.

1.5.0

  • New: “Alert me” on sold-out products in shop and category pages, so shoppers can
    join the back-in-stock list without opening the product. Off until you switch it
    on (Settings > relaybell).
  • New: a subscribe box at the end of your articles, shown only to readers who
    haven’t subscribed. Off until you switch it on; the wording is yours to change.

1.4.0

  • New: order updates. On the thank-you page, buyers can ask to be told about their
    order by notification; relaybell then sends “confirmed”, “shipped”, “out for
    delivery” and “delivered” (each once) as the order’s status changes. Off until
    you turn on Store messages in your relaybell dashboard. Reports a new
    order.status_changed event (switch under Settings → relaybell).
  • New: cash-on-delivery check. With it on in relaybell, a cash-on-delivery buyer
    who opted in gets one notification to confirm the order with a tap, and
    optionally a link to pay online instead.
  • New: cart reminders can show the shopper’s real cart: cart.updated now carries
    up to 10 products (name, image, link, price, quantity), the item count and the
    currency.
  • New: Coming soon (relaybell) checkbox on a product’s Inventory tab. Its
    “Notify me” button reads “Notify me when it launches”, and the first restock
    goes out as a launch message.
  • New: low-stock alerts. When a managed stock count drops to 50 or fewer, a
    low_stock event lets relaybell tell the people who viewed or carted the
    product, once each, when it reaches your threshold (default 5). Switch under
    Settings → relaybell.
  • Order updates are tied to your shop’s address, so a staging copy of your site
    never sends updates to your real buyers.

1.3.0

  • New: personalized recommendations. Your published WooCommerce products and blog
    posts are sent to relaybell’s catalog — the public details only (title, link,
    image, price, category, brand, tags, a short summary, stock) — so notifications
    can recommend the right product or post to each subscriber. Two switches under
    Settings → relaybell → Personalization, both on by default.
  • New: the catalog is sent in the background by WP-Cron, 100 items per run,
    resuming where it stopped; publishing, editing, unpublishing, trashing or
    deleting a product or post, and stock changes, reach relaybell within about a
    minute. Saving never waits for relaybell. A Sync now button and a status in
    plain words (last full sync, items sent, last error).
  • New: reading activity. For subscribed visitors, single posts record
    content.viewed, and content.read once the reader scrolled 75% of the page or
    stayed 30 seconds.
  • New: product.viewed now carries the product’s category, price, currency,
    brand, page address and image, and is recorded while Price drop or “Send my
    products” is on.
  • New: purchase and checkout.started now carry the order number and the
    products bought (id, name, category, price, quantity — up to 50);
    order.refunded carries the order number.
  • New: Import the last 90 days of orders (optional, WooCommerce): past paid
    orders give recommendations a head start. Only orders from customers who already
    get your notifications are kept, running it again never counts an order twice,
    and an imported order isn’t sent again when its status changes later.
  • New: suggested privacy policy text (Settings → Privacy → Policy guide) saying
    what relaybell receives about subscribers and customers.
  • New: filters relaybell_catalog_post_types, relaybell_catalog_item_type,
    relaybell_catalog_item and relaybell_catalog_brand_taxonomies.
  • Change: after updating, the first visit to wp-admin starts one full catalog
    sync in the background.
  • Docs: the plugin page describes every feature, and “External services” lists
    the new catalog, reading-activity and import requests.

1.2.6

  • Change: the “Connect relaybell” and “account email isn’t verified” notices now
    appear only on the Plugins screen, only for administrators, and can be dismissed
    for good. They no longer appear on the Dashboard. Settings → relaybell keeps
    showing the same status.

1.2.5

  • Change: the settings page’s styles and scripts are now regular files
    (assets/relaybell-admin.css, assets/relaybell-admin.js,
    assets/relaybell-notice.js) loaded through WordPress’s script and style
    queues, instead of being printed into the page. The page works exactly as
    before.
  • Change: the “Notify me when back in stock” button’s markup is escaped when it
    is printed.
  • Fix: the status panel now says “1 subscriber” instead of “1 subscribers”.
  • Change: the status panel checks that the relaybell script is reachable without
    running it in wp-admin, and the Disconnect confirmation is part of the
    settings script.
  • Change: the relaybell host (Advanced) must be an https:// address, and the
    home-page cache check keeps TLS certificate checks on.
  • Change: the clean-up that runs when you delete the plugin uses prepared
    database queries. It removes the same data as before.
  • Docs: “External services” now lists every request, including the opt-in
    prompt and on-site message stats, topic preferences, test devices and
    cancelling the API key on disconnect.
  • Docs: older changelog entries moved to changelog.txt.

1.2.4

  • Security: someone could send relaybell a logged-in customer’s email from their
    own browser and then get that customer’s notifications (cart reminders and other
    personal pushes). Your site now signs each logged-in visitor’s ID with a secret
    only your server and relaybell know, and the plugin turns on relaybell’s User ID
    verification for your project, so an ID without a valid signature is ignored.
    It picks up the secret when you connect, when you open Settings → relaybell, and
    once a day. Nothing to set up.
  • New: a status row on Settings → relaybell says whether visitor sign-in IDs are
    verified.
  • New: relaybell_user_hash() for themes and plugins that pass their own IDs to
    relaybell.

Older versions are listed in changelog.txt in the plugin folder.

short_description: Web push for WordPress & WooCommerce: personalized product and post recommendations, cart reminders, back-in-stock alerts and automations.
description:
relaybell turns visitors into subscribers you can bring back with one click — no
app, and no email address needed. A notification reaches them even when your site
isn’t open, and each one can carry the product or post that this subscriber is
likely to want, picked from what they viewed, read and bought on your site.

Connect in about a minute. Then new posts go out as a push when you publish,
abandoned carts get a reminder, sold-out products tell their waitlist when they’re
back, and you see which notifications brought visitors and sales back.

relaybell is free with every feature for up to 500 subscribers; bigger lists have
monthly plans (see https://relaybell.com/pricing).

What you get

  • More returning visitors, without paying for every click.
  • Sales you’d otherwise lose: cart reminders showing the shopper’s own items,
    back-in-stock, price-drop, low-stock and launch alerts go out on their own.
  • Order updates by notification: buyers opt in on the thank-you page and hear
    when their order is confirmed, shipped and delivered; cash-on-delivery orders
    can be confirmed with one tap.
  • Notifications people open: recommendations matched to each subscriber,
    delivered at the hour they usually read.
  • Written and timed by AI: ready-made automations write each message and send
    it when that shopper usually looks.
  • Clear numbers: delivered, clicked and revenue for every notification.
  • Honest numbers: switch on a comparison group to see the sales relaybell
    really added.

Features

Grow subscribers

  • One-click Connect to relaybell — sign in or create a free account, approve
    your site, done. Nothing to copy or paste.
  • Opt-in prompt as a slide-in, bar, modal or the browser’s own prompt; shown after
    a delay, on scroll, on exit intent or on a click; A/B-test its wording.
  • Topics subscribers choose, and an “Alert me when it’s back” button (it reads
    “Alert me when it launches” on products marked Coming soon (relaybell)).
  • Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Samsung Internet and Brave on desktop and Android;
    Safari on macOS 13+ and on iPhone/iPad (iOS 16.4+, from the Home Screen).

Personalized notifications

  • Catalog sync: published WooCommerce products and blog posts are sent to
    relaybell in the background and updated within about a minute of each change.
  • Per-subscriber interests, learned from what each subscriber views, reads,
    adds to the cart and buys on your site — your own first-party data only.
  • Product and article recommendations: put {rec.title}, {rec.price} or
    {rec.summary} in a notification and each subscriber gets their own pick.
    Out-of-stock products are skipped at send time.
  • GA4 events with no code: relaybell can use the Google Analytics 4
    e-commerce events your site already sends through Google Tag Manager or gtag.js.
  • Smart timing: delivery at each subscriber’s usual hour, in their time zone,
    within your quiet hours and frequency cap.
  • Past orders (optional): import 90 days of orders for a head start.

Automations & journeys

  • Push new posts on publish, with the featured image, for the post types you pick.
  • Welcome series and custom journeys with delays and branches; subscribers leave
    when they buy.
  • Automations triggered by anything a subscriber does on your site.
  • Recurring campaigns, RSS-to-push, scheduling and A/B-tested notifications.

WooCommerce

  • Cart reminders for shoppers who added to cart or started checkout.
  • Back in stock alerts to the product’s waitlist.
  • Price drop alerts to shoppers who viewed, carted or wait-listed it.
  • Order updates: thank-you and follow-up messages after purchases and refunds.
  • Revenue attribution, with each order counted once.
  • Classic checkout, the Checkout block and HPOS.

Analytics & delivery health

  • Delivered, clicks, conversions and revenue per notification; CSV export.
  • Delivery health: why a notification didn’t arrive, in plain words.
  • Conversion goals with a funnel.

Privacy & control

  • Consent: Google Consent Mode, or wait for your cookie banner’s consent.
  • GDPR: export or erase everything held about a subscriber.
  • Identity verification: logged-in visitors’ IDs are signed by your server, so
    nobody can pose as a customer to get their notifications. On from the start.
  • A switch for each WooCommerce event and for catalog sync.
  • Suggested privacy policy text for your site, under Settings → Privacy.

Works with

WooCommerce, Google Tag Manager and GA4, Zapier, the relaybell REST API and
webhooks, server SDKs for Node.js and PHP, and common page-cache plugins.

Why relaybell

  • Set up in about a minute: one click, no keys, no code, no theme changes.
  • It checks itself: the status panel tests eight things — connection, HTTPS,
    the script, the service worker, your browser, your public pages, page caches
    and sign-in IDs — and says how to fix anything that isn’t right.
  • Never slows your site: events are sent after the page is built; the catalog
    and past orders go out in small background batches; saving a post never waits
    for relaybell.
  • Built for real hosting: the service worker is a static file in the plugin
    folder (no clash with PWA plugins, any permalink setting), its address avoids
    patterns hosting firewalls block, and 13 common page caches are cleared when
    your set-up changes.
  • Secure by default: signed visitor IDs, HTTPS-only connection settings, and
    the API key is cancelled when you disconnect.
  • Open: GPL plugin, documented REST API and webhooks, CSV export.

Your data

Nothing is sent until you connect. The catalog holds only what is public on your
site — never password-protected, private or hidden items, and no customer data.
Activity is recorded only for visitors who subscribed. Order events carry the
customer’s email (or your hashed ID) only to find their subscription — no names,
addresses or phone numbers. Past orders are sent only when you ask. Every request
is listed under “External services”.

External services

This plugin connects to relaybell (https://relaybell.com), a web push
notification service operated by Nexistech. relaybell is required: browser push
notifications can’t be stored or delivered without a push service, and this
plugin is the WordPress client for it. You need a relaybell account and API key.

1. Browser SDK (https://relaybell.com/relaybell-sdk.js)

Loaded on every front-end page once a Project ID is saved, so visitors can opt in.
On each page view it also fetches your project’s public settings (GET
https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/config: push key, prompt and
on-site message settings). Browsers send their normal request data (IP address,
user agent, your site’s address). If you use them, it also reports, without
personal data, which A/B prompt version was shown (POST …/prompt-event) and
on-site message views and clicks (POST …/onsite-event).

2. Subscribing (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/subscriptions)

When a visitor accepts the notification prompt: the browser’s push endpoint URL
and encryption keys, the page URL, language, time zone, prompt version, and your
topics or tags (for logged-in users, their WordPress role). The service worker
re-sends a subscription the browser replaced. Topic choices made in the box
opened by RelayBell.showPreferences() are saved (GET/POST …/preferences).
For a logged-in visitor (never an administrator) who opted in, their account email
is sent as externalId, with a userHash signature (see 9). Hash it with the
relaybell_external_id filter, or turn off “Link subscribers to their account
email”.

3. Publish pushes (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications)

With “Send on publish” on: the post’s title, first 20 words, permalink, featured
image URL and (with “Category → topic”) topic. Never for password-protected posts.

4. WooCommerce events from your server (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/events)

With your API key, at the end of the request that caused them: purchase and
checkout.started (order id and number, total, currency, the payment method’s id
such as “cod”, and up to 50 products: id, name, category, unit price, quantity); order.refunded (order id and number,
amount, currency); order.status_changed (order id and number, the new and old
status, your shop’s address, and for a registered customer the “view order” page
address); cart.updated (the added product’s name, id and URL, cart value and
currency, and up to 10 cart products: id, name, image URL, page URL, price,
quantity); signup (user id); back_in_stock (product name, id, URL, and whether
it was marked Coming soon), price_drop (product name, id, URL, and old and new
price) and low_stock (product name, id, URL and stock count, when a managed
stock count falls to 50 or fewer). All on by default; each can be turned off
under Settings → relaybell. While “Link subscribers to their account email”
is on, the customer’s email (account email, else the billing email, or your
relaybell_external_id value) is sent with purchase, checkout.started,
order.status_changed, cart.updated, signup and order.refunded; with it
off, they’re sent without it and cart.updated not at all. cart.updated is only
sent for logged-in shoppers. back_in_stock, price_drop and low_stock never
include customer data.

5. Visitor activity (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/projects/{project id}/events)

From the browser, only for visitors subscribed to your notifications:
waitlist.join (the “Notify me” button), product.viewed (a product page, while
Price drop or “Send my products” is on: product id, category, price, currency,
brand, page URL, image) and content.viewed (a post, while “Send my posts” is
on: post id, title, type, category, up to 10 tags, permalink), followed once by
content.read when they scrolled 75% of the page or stayed 30 seconds, and
search_submitted (on a search results page, while the “Still looking for…?”
automation is on in relaybell, for visitors subscribed to your notifications or
signed in: the words searched and the results page address with only its search
parameters; words that look like an email address, a phone number or a link are not
kept). Each
carries your project id, the push endpoint URL and, for a logged-in visitor with
“Link subscribers…” on, their externalId and userHash.

On the order-received (thank-you) page, while order updates are on in your
relaybell dashboard, the buyer can choose “Yes, notify me”: their browser sends
(POST …/projects/{project id}/order-link) the push endpoint URL and the order’s
id and number, payment method, total, currency, status, your shop’s address and
time, signed on your server with your identity secret (see 9). The signed order is
printed in that page only with the order’s own key in the address, and never for
failed, cancelled or refunded orders. No name, email or address is included.

6. Delivery and click reports (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/notifications/{id}/receipt and /click)

From the service worker: the notification id, a signed token and the
subscription’s id — no page content or personal data.

7. Connecting (https://relaybell.com/connect/wordpress, POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/connect/exchange)

Connect to relaybell sends the administrator’s browser to relaybell with your
site’s address and name, the wp-admin return address and a one-time security
value. Your server then trades the one-time code (with your site address) for
your Project ID and an API key, saved in your database.

8. Admin status and test push (https://relaybell.com/api/v1/…)

From your server, with your API key: subscriber count (GET /stats), that the
Project ID matches the key (GET /me), and when relaybell last ran on your pages
(GET /setup-status); the Plugins screen re-checks an unverified account at most
hourly. The administrator’s browser fetches the script and public settings to
check they aren’t blocked, and your server occasionally fetches your own home page
to detect a stale page cache (that request stays on your site). Subscribe this
browser subscribes the admin’s browser (see 2) and marks it as a test device
(POST /test-devices: its endpoint URL); Send test push sends a test to test
devices only (POST /test-devices/send: test title, text, home page address); a
“send test to my device” link registers that browser (POST /test-devices/claim:
the code and endpoint URL). Advanced → relaybell host changes where these
requests go (https only).

9. Identity verification (GET and PUT https://relaybell.com/api/v1/identity)

Your server fetches your project’s identity secret — when you connect, when you
open Settings → relaybell, and daily — and the first time asks relaybell to
accept only verified sign-in IDs (changeable in your relaybell dashboard). The
secret signs logged-in visitors’ IDs on your server and never appears in your
pages. No visitor data is sent.

10. Disconnecting (DELETE https://relaybell.com/api/v1/keys/current)

Disconnect cancels the API key one-click Connect created (only the key is
sent). A key entered by hand is left alone.

11. Catalog (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/catalog/items and /catalog/items/delete)

So notifications can recommend them, your server sends the public details of
published WooCommerce products (“Send my products”) and posts (“Send my posts”),
both on by default: id, title, permalink, image URL, price and sale price with
the currency, category path, brand, tags, a short plain-text summary, stock
status and publication date. Never password-protected, private, draft or hidden
items, and no customer data. WP-Cron sends them in the background, 100 per run:
everything when you connect, update the plugin, change these settings or click
Sync now, and weekly; and each product or post you publish, edit,
unpublish, trash or delete within about a minute (for the last three, only its
id). Turning a switch off removes those items from relaybell.

12. Past orders (POST https://relaybell.com/api/v1/events/import)

Only after an administrator clicks Import the last 90 days of orders: that
period’s paid orders as purchase events, 50 per background run — the details of
a live purchase (see 4), the payment date, and the customer’s email (or your
relaybell_external_id value) to find their subscription. relaybell keeps only
orders of customers who already get your notifications, never counts an order
twice, and gets no names, addresses or phone numbers.

Nothing is sent until you connect (or save a Project ID and API key manually).

Privacy policy: https://relaybell.com/privacy

upgrade_notice.1.10.0: Tells relaybell when a payment fails, with the order's pay-again link, for the optional "Payment didn't go through" reminder. Nothing else changes.
upgrade_notice.1.9.0: Sends each order's payment method id (such as "cod") so relaybell can ask cash-on-delivery buyers to pay online, if you turn that on. Nothing else changes.
upgrade_notice.1.8.0: Sends tracked stock counts with your products, so relaybell's optional "Only 3 left" note can show real numbers. Nothing else changes.
upgrade_notice.1.7.0: Lets relaybell add a one-time WooCommerce discount code to cart reminders and welcome messages. Nothing changes until you turn discounts on in relaybell.
upgrade_notice.1.6.0: A simpler settings page and a one-line status check. Your settings stay as they are.
upgrade_notice.1.5.0: Two optional new places to ask: "Alert me" on sold-out products in shop pages, and a subscribe box at the end of articles. Both are off until you switch them on.
upgrade_notice.1.4.0: Order updates and cash-on-delivery checks by notification, cart reminders with the shopper's own items, Coming soon products and low-stock alerts. New features stay off until you turn them on in relaybell.
upgrade_notice.1.3.0: Personalized recommendations: your public products and posts are sent to relaybell in the background (two switches under Settings → relaybell → Personalization), and order events now include the products bought.
upgrade_notice.1.2.6: The relaybell notices now show only on the Plugins screen and can be dismissed. No settings change.
upgrade_notice.1.2.5: Maintenance release: the settings page loads its script and styles as files, and the readme lists every request the plugin makes. No settings change.
